title: Text: building a word counter
summary: Work with std::string and char: transform text, split it into words, read whole lines, and write a palindrome checker judged by hidden tests.

steps.title: Characters and loops over strings
hints: Make a copy (`std::string result = text;`), change the copy's characters, return it.
`for (char& c : result)` — the `&` makes `c` refer to the actual character inside `result`, so assigning to `c` changes the string.

steps.title: Splitting text into words
hints: Keep a `std::string current`. For each character: if it's a letter or digit, append it (`current += c`). Otherwise, if `current` isn't empty, it's a finished word — `push_back` it and `clear()` it.
Don't forget the last word: after the loop, `current` may still hold one.

steps.title: A command-line word counter
commands: cmake --build build && printf 'Hello world\nC++ is fun\n' | ./build/words
hints: `while (std::getline(std::cin, line))` reads one whole line per iteration, without the newline.
Characters per line: `line.size()`. Words per line: `split_words(line).size()`.

quiz.question: What is the difference between `'a'` and `"a"` in C++?
options: None — both are one-character strings, like in Python.
`'a'` is a single `char` (one byte holding a number, 97); `"a"` is a string literal: an array of two chars, 'a' followed by a terminating '\0'.
explanations: In Python they're interchangeable. In C++ they are different *types*, and mixing them up produces confusing compiler errors.

Right. A `char` is a small integer — that's why `std::tolower` works on it and why `'a' + 1` is `98`. A string literal is a fixed array of `char`s ending with `'\0'`; it becomes a `std::string` only when you convert it, e.g. `std::string s = "a";`.
It's the other way round, and neither is a `std::string` by itself.
A literal like `"a"` is a plain array of characters (`const char[2]`), not a `std::string`. That's why `"Hello, " + "world"` doesn't compile but `std::string("Hello, ") + "world"` does.

steps.title: Challenge: palindromes

checks.label: Hidden acceptance tests pass
checks.failMessage: Your tests pass, but the hidden tests found a case is_palindrome gets wrong. Think about capital letters, punctuation, empty text and single characters.

hints: First build a cleaned-up string holding only the lower-cased letters and digits. Then compare it with itself from both ends.
Two indices: `i` from the front, `j` from the back. While they haven't met, compare `letters[i]` with `letters[j - 1]`.
Careful with `std::size_t` (unsigned) and going below zero: `j - 1` when `j == 0` wraps around to a huge number. Using `i + 1 < j` as the loop condition avoids it.
